text:
JL 3124

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-05-053073-993

DATE:

OCTOBER 22, 2002

______________________________________________________________________

BY:

THE HONOURABLE

HÉLÈNE LANGLOIS, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

MICHAEL CHERNACK

Plaintiff

v.

AIR FRANCE

and

JOËL CORNELOUP

Defendants

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Plaintiff seeks Defendants' condemnation in the
amount of $150,000 for punitive damages.  He alleges they have violated his
fundamental right to practice his religion in interrupting and preventing him
to continue his morning prayers while he was travelling from Montreal to Paris
on an Air France flight. Defendants deny such a fact.

[
2
]

Defendants have not, at any time, contested the
Court's lack of jurisdiction
rationae personae
; this implies their
submission to the Court's jurisdiction
[1]
.

[
3
]

The questions at issue are the following:

•

Does the Warsaw Convention apply?

•

If not, on what basis can Plaintiff justify his
claim:  the
Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
(The Charter) as
pleaded by Plaintiff or the Canadian Human Rights Act (the Code) as pleaded by
Defendants;

•

If the Code applies, does the Court have
jurisdiction?  Air France pleads that in such case the Human Rights Tribunal
has exclusive jurisdiction over the matter;

•

If the Court is competent to hear the matter,
was there violation of Plaintiff's fundamental right to practice his religion?
In the affirmative, was it intentional?

THE FACT

[
4
]

On April 25
th
, 1999,
Mr. Chernack is a passenger on Air France flight 347, travelling from
Montreal to Paris, the final destination being a return to Montreal.
Mr. Corneloup is chief steward on the plane; he is employed by Air France.

[
5
]

Mr. Chernack, a sales agent in the textile
business, travels to Europe 3 to 4 times a year. On that day, he travels
accompanied by a business associate and friend who sits beside him.  The flight
is full.

[
6
]

Mr. Chernack is of the Jewish faith and
describes himself as an observant Jew.  He, therefore, follows as much as
possible the rules of his religion known as the Commandments.  According to
Mr. Chenack's understanding, they impose upon him the obligation to
proceed every day, between sunrise until late morning, to the morning prayers.
The prayers ritual are standard Jewish law and cannot be derogated from.  The
morning prayers ritual on April 25,1999, a Monday, was expected to lasts
approximately 40 to 45 minutes.

[
7
]

Mr. Chernack
testified
that between 1:30 to 2 hours prior to landing, approximately 7:15 Paris time,
he proceeded to the back of the plane to pray.  The projection of the movie on
the plane had ended and the lights had been shut down. Most passengers seemed
to be resting or sleeping. It appeared the most appropriate time for him to
pray taking into consideration his travel arrangements and schedule.

[
8
]

He, therefore, walked up the left aisle (looking
at the front of the plane) and identified on the left side, close to the back
of the plane near the washrooms, a location just beside an emergency door, he
refers to as an "alcove".  This is where he proceeded to his morning
payers.  The area was dimly lit and considered a sensitive zone on the
aircraft.

[
9
]

Mr. Chernack did not verify with Air France
personnel whether he could pray or if this was a convenient place to pray; he
had prayed previously on other flights, including Air France flights, without
having been advised not to do so.

[
10
]

The praying process involves the donning of the
prayer shawl and phylacteries, all noticeable.  While praying, Mr. Chernack
held a prayers book and was standing facing the window, his back to the aisles
and the passengers. He read the prayers in a hushed undertone, producing a very
soft whisper.

[
11
]

When he had reached a time of approximately less
than five minutes into the prayers where he is forbidden to converse or
interact with any outside influence, except a life-threatening event, Mr.
Chernack felt a gentle tap on his left side.  He turned and saw
Mr. Corneloup, speaking to him, in French.

[
12
]

At his examination on discovery, Mr. Chernack
recalled Mr. Corneloup saying:
«C'est un avion ici,
c'est pas une place pour les pratiques d'occulte.  Retournez à votre siège
immédiatement»
[2]
.

[
13
]

At the hearing, he admitted his limited
knowledge of French and was not anymore certain of what exactly was said to
him: the word "occulte" may have been "de culte".  At the
time Mr. Chernack understood, he was being told that it was not a place to
pray.  In shock, he stared at Mr. Corneloup without responding.

[
14
]

Mr. Corneloup continued to walk down the aisle a
few feet ahead, came back and repeated «
Retournez à
votre siège immédiatement.»
The order was given in
a harsh, rude and threatening manner and seemed to emanate from someone in
authority.  Mr. Corneloup then stormed away and did not return.

[
15
]

There remained approximately 30 minutes of
prayers to be read.  Mr. Chernack who did not want another confrontation, moved
to a corridor joining the two aisles at the back of the plane; nervously and in
rush he continued and completed his prayers.

[
16
]

After returning to his seat, he summoned
Mr. Corneloup to meet him.  The latter offered his excuses and explained
that praying was not permitted on the airplane as it was against Air France's
policy.  He went on distinguishing between domestic and international flights
but Mr. Chernack does not specifically recall what was said as he had ceased
paying attention. He was upset and asked Mr. Corneloup to provide him with his
name and badge number, which he did.  He then informed Mr. Corneloup that he
would hear from his attorney.

[
17
]

Mr. Chernack does not recall discussing the
matter with any other Air France representative.

[
18
]

In a note he wrote immediately after the
incident, Mr. Chernack mentioned that Mr. Corneloup «
returned minutes later
& apologized, stating that he had erred in that on long-term flights prayer
was
permissable, but he didn't know this as he
was a short-term AF flight person
».
[3]

[
19
]

Breakfast was served approximately 10 to 15
minutes after; he ordered and was served a kosher meal.

•

[
20
]

Mr. Corneloup
testified
that on April 25, 1999, he had been working with Air France for 18 years and
had recently started to work on international flights; previously, he worked on
domestic flights.

[
21
]

In preparation for breakfast he walked up the
right aisle and proceeded to wake up the Air France personnel still resting in
a reserved area at the back of the plane.  According to standard routine, the
personnel resting is usually awaken 5 to 10 minutes before breakfast is
served.  Mr. Corneloup then walked by passengers standing near the washrooms,
advised them that breakfast would soon be served and invited them to return to
their seats.  He verified the washrooms and he proceeded to walk down the left
aisle.  He did not immediately notice Mr.  Chernack, his view being
obstructed.  It is only when he walked by him that he saw Mr. Chernack but did
not noticed the shawl he was wearing.  Still walking, he put his hand on Mr.
Chernack's left shoulder and invited him to return to his seat.  Mr. Chernack
turned around.  It is then that he realized he was praying.  Mr. Corneloup,
uncomfortable, apologized and tried to explain why he had disturbed him.  He
said:  «
Je suis désolé.  Je vous ai dérangé.  C'est un avion.
Vous comprenez qu'on ne peut pas y avoir la quiétude d'un lieu
d'église.  On ne peut pas avoir, ce n'est pas un lieu de culte.  On ne peut pas
avoir la quiétude d'un lieu de culte.».
[4]

[
22
]

He did not order Mr. Chernack to stop praying.
He only tried to make him understand that his seat was a more appropriate place
to pray, in the circumstances. He was unaware that the prayers have to be done
while standing.

[
23
]

Later on when he met again Mr. Chernack, he
apologized for having unfortunately interrupted his prayers and explained that
he used to work on Air France domestic flights where he had not been accustomed
to witness people praying while standing.

[
24
]

Mr. Corneloup does not recall discussing any of
Air France policies.

•

[
25
]

Dominique Ramspacher,
on April 25, 1999, was exceptionally on board Air France flight
347.  As flight instructor, he was there to validate the trial period of some
members of the crew, including Mr. Corneloup who had just recently been
transferred from domestic to international flights.

[
26
]

He was informed of the incident involving Mr.
Chernack by Mr. Corneloup just before breakfast was served. He himself went to
meet Mr. Chernack, apologized for the incident and tried on two occasions
to engage in a conversation with him but the latter refused.

[
27
]

Should the situation arise where a passenger
expresses a need to pray during a flight, Air France personnel was instructed
to act according to the situation but in all cases try, as much as possible, to
accommodate the passenger.

[
28
]

The resting area reserved for Air France flight
personnel, at the rear of the plane, is located not far from where
Mr. Chernack prayed at first; it remains most of the time unoccupied and
may be used to accommodate passengers who wish to pray.

•

[
29
]

Non contradicted evidence is to the effect that
Air France has no policy, whether written or non-written, prohibiting prayers
on its aircrafts.

•

The Warsaw Convention

[
30
]

The pertinent provisions of the "Act to
give effect to a Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules Relating to
International Carriage by Air"
[5]
, known
as the Warsaw Convention (Convention) are the following:

«
Art. 17:
The carrier is liable for damage sustained in the
event of the death or wounding of a passenger or any other bodily injury
suffered by a passenger, if the accident which caused the damage so sustained
took place on board the aircraft or in the course of any of the operations of
embarking or disembarking.

Art. 24
:  (1)  In the cases covered by Articles 18 and 19 any
action for damages, however founded, can only be brought subject to the
conditions and limits set out in this Convention.

(2)  In the cases covered by Article 17
the provisions of the preceding paragraph also apply, without prejudice to the
questions as to who are persons who have the right to bring suit and what are
their respective rights.

Art. 28:
(1)  An action for damages must be brought, at the
option of the plaintiff, in the territory of one of the High Contracting
Parties, either before the Court having jurisdiction where the carrier is
ordinarily resident, or has his principal place of business, or has an
establishment by which the contract has been made or before the Court having
jurisdiction at the place of destination.

(2)  Questions of procedure shall be governed by the law
of the Court seized of the case.»

[
31
]

According to Art. 1 of the Convention, it
applies
«to all international carriage of persons, baggage or cargo
performed by aircraft for reward.»
[6]

It provides remedy to a Plaintiff seeking compensation for damages, as
contemplated by Art. 17, that is, for bodily injury suffered.  With respect to
the meaning of bodily injury, whether the issue is looked at in light of the
objectives of the Convention or the definition of bodily injury according to
Quebec Law (
lex fori
), the end result is to the effect that the
Convention does not offer remedy for moral or punitive damages.

[
32
]

Indeed:

«The object of the convention is to
provide compensation to plaintiffs who have suffered loss, subject to the
defences and limitations it sets out.  In the English courts, the question of
exemplary or punitive damages will seldom arise but it is submitted that the
convention contemplates only the award of compensation for damage actually
sustained by the plaintiff and excludes non-compensatory claims.  This
submission rests both on the  general objectives of the convention and the
proper interpretation of its provisions.

The expectation of the contracting parties who negotiated the Warsaw
Convention was that it would establish a uniform limit on an airline carrier's
liability, a strict limit but one of which would ensure a proper measure of
compensation for those suffering loss.  There is nothing in the drafting
history of the Convention to suggest that its authors ever contemplated the
availability of punitive damages; indeed in civil law countries, where the
claims would normally sound in contract, punitive damages would not be
available.

It has been held, it is submitted
rightly, that the damages contemplated by art 17 are purely compensatory.»
[7]

[
33
]

Mr. Justice Sharpe of the Ontario Court of
justice, in
Linda Naval-Torres
v.
Northwest Airlines Inc
.
[8]
, while discussing the application of the
Convention to the damage claim filed by Mrs. Naval-Torres, wrote that:

«The
Convention
focuses on particular harms and prescribes
rights and remedies which may be exercised in the event those harms are
suffered.

[…]

In my view, it is clearly established that where the plaintiff's claim
falls within the
Warsaw Convention
, no claim for punitive damages may be
advanced and that the plaintiff does not escape that constraint by alleging
intentional wrongdoing.

Punitive damages are not compensatory, bur rather designed to punish:
see
Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
(1995),
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
,
126 D.L.R. (4
th
)
129
at 185-6
per Cory J.: "Punitive damages bear no relation to what the
plaintiff should receive by way of compensation.  Their aim is not to
compensate the plaintiff, but rather to punish the defendant."  Article 17
provides only for liability for "damage sustained".  This language
indicates that damages to be awarded under the
Convention
are
compensatory in nature.  While I was referred to no Canadian or English cases
on the point, American courts appear to have been unanimous in accepting the
contention that only compensatory damages are permitted by the
Convention

and that punitive damages are excluded; see
Re Air Disaster at Lockerbie
Scotland on Dec. 21,
1988
, 928 F.2d 1267
(2
nd
Cir, 1991);
Re
Korean Airlines Disaster of Sept 1,
1993
932, F. 2e 1475
(D.C. Cir. 1991)
,
cert. denied 112 S. Ct. 616 (1991).»

[
34
]

Finally, under Quebec Law, Mr. Justice Jules
Deschênes in the case of
Dame Surprenant
v.
Air Canada
[9]
, and the Supreme Court in the case of
Ville
de Verdun
v.
Gilles Doré
[10]
held
that damage sustained in the event of bodily injury would not include punitive
damages.

[
35
]

The Court therefore concludes that the
Convention does not apply and the Court's competence over the present matter cannot
be determined on the basis of Art. 28 of the Convention as pleaded by
Plaintiff.

THE
CHARTER

[
36
]

Article 55
of the
Charter
provides that:

«The Charter affects those matters that come under the legislative
authority of Quebec.»

[
37
]

In
Irwin Toys Ltd.
v
Attorney General
of Quebec
[11]
,
the Supreme Court held that:

«The federal government has exclusive jurisdiction as regards
"essential and vital elements" of a federal undertaking, including
the management of such an undertaking, because those matters form the
"basic, minimum and unassailable content" of the head of power
created by operation of s. 91(29) and the exceptions in
s. 92(10)
of the
Constitution
Act. 1867
.  No provincial law touching on those matters can apply to a
federal undertaking.  However, where provincial legislation does not purport to
apply to a federal undertaking, its incidental effect, even upon a vital part
of the operation of the undertaking, will not normally render the provincial
legislation
ultra vires.»

[
38
]

Aeronautics and air transportation have been
found within the exclusive legislative authority of Parliament. More
specifically on the subject, the Supreme Court in
Air Canada
v.

Ontario (Liquor Control Board)

[12]
,
held :

«This Court has defined the scope
of the federal aeronautics' power by reference to the physical act of flight.
Aeronautics is :

The flight and period of flight from the time the machine clears the
earth to the time it returns successfully to the earth and is resting securely
on the ground.

Johannesson v. Rural
Municipality of West St. Paul
, [1952] S.C.R. 292,
at p. 319.  Thus the federal aeronautics jurisdiction encompasses not only the
regulation of the operation of aircraft, but also the regulation of the
operation of airports.[...]  By contrast, laws that affect matters incidental
to the operation of aircraft – for example, laws that affect the operation of
an airport limousine service – have not run afoul of the "integral
part" doctrine.  See e.g.,
Murray Hill Limousine Service Ltd. V. Batson

[1965] Que. Q.B. 778. ».

[
39
]

The Court finds that, in the present case, the
alleged violation of Plaintiff's fundamental right occurred in the context of
the management of the aircraft during the period of flight, an essential and
vital element of Federal undertaking and  concludes that the
Charter
is
inapplicable as regards Plaintiff's action and cannot serve as basis therefore.

THE COURT'S
COMPETENCE

[
40
]

Air France has chosen not to raise the issue as
to whether or not the Convention is «
exhaustive of the rights of passengers
who assert claims arising during the course of international carriage by air
[13]
»
.

[
41
]

Air France argues that Articles 8 and 14 of the
Code may serve as basis to Plaintiff's claim for punitive damages but the
administration and implementation of the Code has been vested exclusively in
the Canadian Human Rights Commission and, ultimately, in the Canadian Human
Rights Tribunal (the Tribunal).

[
42
]

The Court disagrees.

[
43
]

In
Attorney

General of 'Ontario
v

Pembina Exploration Canada Ltd.
[14]
,
Justice Laforest writes:

«It is clear to me that the provincial power over the administration of
justice in the province enables a province to invest its superior courts with
jurisdiction over the full range of cases, whether the applicable law is
federal, provincial or constitutional [...].

[…]

[...] if federal law calls for the exercise of adjudication but is
silent as to forum, the provincial courts are clearly competent to adjudicate.
In a word, judicial jurisdiction is not tied to provincial legislative
jurisdiction in other areas.

[
44
]

Indeed, Provincial Superior Courts are presumed
competent unless jurisdiction is assigned exclusively to another Court by a
specific provision of Law.
[15]
»

[
45
]

The Code does not include a provision investing
the Tribunal with exclusive jurisdiction over the application and interpretation
of the Code.

[
46
]

The Human Rights Commission and the Tribunal, as
a result of the «
legislative intention to create administrative bodies which
can deal with issues in an economically efficient and expeditious fashion»
[16]
,
acquired jurisdiction over human rights
matters however while Provincial Superior Courts remained competent over these
matters.

[
47
]

Mr. Chernack chose to seize the Court with
respect to his action instead of filing a complaint with the Human Rights
Commission and he was entitled to do so.

DID
DEFENDANTS VIOLATE PLAINTIFF'S FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT TO PRACTICE HIS RELIGION?

[
48
]

The pertinent dispositions of the Code are the
following:

«
Art. 2
:  The purpose of this Act is to extend the laws in
Canada to give effect, within the purview of matters coming within the
legislative authority of Parliament, to the principle that all individuals
should have an opportunity equal with other individuals to make for themselves
the lives that they are able and wish to have and to have their needs
accommodated, consistent with their duties and obligations as members of
society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory
practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex,
sexual orientation, marital status, family status, disability or conviction for
an offence for which a pardon has been granted.

Art. 3
:  (1)  For all purposes of this Act, the prohibited grounds of
discrimination are race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex,
sexual orientation, marital status, family status, disability and conviction
for which a pardon has been granted.

(
2)  Where the ground of discrimination is pregnancy or
child-birth, the discrimination shall be deemed to be on the ground of se
x.»

[
49
]

Justice Dixon for the majority of the Supreme
Court in
R
. v
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
[17]
, defined the concept of freedom of
religion in the following manner:

«Freedom must surely be founded in respect for the inherent dignity and
the inviolable rights of the human person.  The essence of the concept of
freedom of religion is the right to entertain such religious beliefs as a
person chooses, the right to declare religious beliefs openly and without fear
of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to manifest religious belief by worship
and practice or by teaching and dissemination.  But the concept means more than
that.

Freedom can primarily be characterized by the absence
of coercion or constraint.  If a person is compelled by the state or the will
of another to a course of action or inaction which he would not otherwise have
chosen, he is not acting of his own volition and he cannot be said to be truly
free.  One of the major purposes of the
Charter
is to protect, within
reason, from compulsion or restraint
.  Coercion includes not only such blatant forms of
compulsion as direct commands to act or refrain from acting on pain of
sanction, coercion includes indirect forms of control which determine or limit
alternative courses of conduct available to others.  Freedom in a broad sense
embraces both the absence of coercion and constraint, and the right to manifest
beliefs and practices.  Freedom means that, subject to such limitations as are
necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals or the fundamental
rights and freedoms of others, no one is to be forced to act in a way contrary
to his beliefs or his conscience.»

(underlining added)

[
50
]

A person's sincere personal religious beliefs
are to be taken into consideration when such a person pleads her right to
freedom of religion.
[18]

•

[
51
]

Mr. Chernack's personal religious beliefs, which
in essence correspond to the Commandments, are to the effect that the morning
prayers are done standing, involve the donning of the prayer shawl and
phylacteries and must take place at a time between sunrise until late morning.

[
52
]

The evidence also revealed that, notwithstanding
having been interrupted, Mr. Chernack was able to complete his morning
prayers.  However, he did so nervously, in a rush and certainly in a shorter
period of time and without his usual peace of mind.

•

[
53
]

Was it as a result of a discriminatory conduct
by Mr. Corneloup?  The burden relies on Mr. Chernack to establish a case of
discrimination.

[
54
]

The fact that Mr. Corneloup interrupted Mr.
Chernack's prayers cannot be found to be the result, either directly or as an
adverse effect of discrimination, of a policy adopted by Air France prohibiting
prayers on its airplanes:  Air France has no such policy.

[
55
]

There is discrimination:

a) in the presence of a distinction, exclusion or preference,

b) when such distinction, exclusion or preference is based on one or
more of the motives enumerated in the law,

c) when the distinction, exclusion or preference caused prejudice in
the sense that there was infringement of essential human integrity.
[19]
Also, «
A person
or group of persons has been discriminated against […] when members of that
group have been

made to feel, […] that they are less capable, or less worthy of
recognition or value as human beings or as members of Canadian society, equally
deserving of concern, respect, and consideration
.»
[20]

[
56
]

The testimonies of Mr. Corneloup, Mr. Chernack
and Mr. Ramspacher, although they vary with respect to time frame, show, in all
likelihood, that Mr. Corneloup acted in the context of preparation for
breakfast:  Mr. Corneloup testified to that effect;  Mr. Ramspacher said
he was informed of the incident during preparation for breakfast and, according
to Mr. Chernack, breakfast was served ten minutes after his second
encounter with Mr. Corneloup which took place soon after he had returned
to his seat.  There is no proof that Mr. Corneloup acted for another
purpose nor is there any evidence justifying this Court to dismiss
Mr. Corneloup's testimony in this respect.  Nowhere in the evidence is
there any indication that, as suggested by Plaintiff, Mr. Corneloup
intended to prevent him from praying because it disturbed him. The fact that
once he had advised Mr. Chernack, Mr. Corneloup did not insist nor did he
return later to verify if Mr. Chernack had moved and the non contradicted
evidence that, as part of his routine, Mr. Corneloup in all likelihood
also invited other standing passengers to return to their seats, tend to
demonstrate otherwise.

[
57
]

Plaintiff argues that Mr. Corneloup knew about
the prayer shawl and, therefore, must have known he was interrupting him in his
prayers.  However, Mr. Corneloup testified that he did not see the shawl
nor did he realize Mr. Chernack was praying prior to the time he turned to
face him.  Again, the evidence do not offer any ground to dismiss such
explanation; such assertion do indeed reconcile with the fact that,

•

the lighting at the location where Mr. Chernack
was standing was dim, as the lights on the plane were still turned off,

•

Mr. Chernack was standing his back to the aisle,

•

when Mr. Corneloup interrupted Mr. Chernack, he
was acting in the context of a routine procedure, while walking down the left
aisle and in all likelihood was not paying attention.

In such
context, Plaintiff 's shawl and phylacteries probably remained unnoticed.

•

[
58
]

Was Mr. Chernack compelled to a situation
where he had to make a choice, and one of those choices was not to pray or to
pray without following the ritual of the morning prayers?

[
59
]

Air France has no policy prohibiting prayers on
its airplanes and, in fact, Plaintiff did pray on other flights including Air
France flights. The airline offered accommodations suitable to allow Plaintiff
to proceed to his morning prayers without being interrupted.  Also, should it
not have been breakfast time, the evidence brings the Court to conclude that
Mr. Chernack, in all probability, would not have been invited to return to
his seat unless the captain signalled otherwise, and this for security
reasons.

[
60
]

The time chosen by Mr. Chernack to pray without
first informing a member of the crew and the misunderstanding between him and
Mr. Corneloup, with respect to the reasons for the interruption, led to an
unfortunate incident

[
61
]

The evidence failed to establish not only a
discriminating conduct on the part of Mr. Corneloup and Air France but
also an intent to cause damage which must be proven in order to succeed in a
claim for punitive damages.
[21]

[
62
]

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
63
]

DISMISSES
the
claim of Michael Chernack against Air France and Joël Corneloup;

[
64
]

WITH COSTS
.
